planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade on a sturdy, permanent trellis, arbor, or pergola; Magnifica's heavier racemes benefit from especially robust support wire from the start.

directions: Magnifica is a long-cultivated, large-flowered selection of American wisteria known in old European nursery and arboretum literature as var. magnifica, distinguished from the wild species by somewhat larger leaflets and denser, showier racemes eight to twelve inches long carrying up to ninety lightly fragrant, mauve-purple flowers apiece. Like other native wisterias it twines and blooms on new growth, so a hard late-winter or post-bloom pruning never costs next year's flowers, and it lacks the aggressive suckering and seed-spreading habit of Chinese and Japanese wisteria. Grow it in ordinary, well-drained garden soil in full sun on a genuinely sturdy permanent structure, since its heavier bloom clusters demand more support than the species type. Once established it is a tough, long-lived, low-maintenance vine tolerant of heat and a wide range of soils.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

common_name: Bayou Two O'Clock Wisteria (Repeat-Blooming Kentucky Wisteria)

planting.note: Plant container vines in late winter or spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade on a sturdy trellis, pergola, or arbor; Bayou Two O'Clock often flowers while still young, well ahead of seed-grown wisteria.

directions: Bayou Two O'Clock is a Louisiana-collected selection of native Kentucky wisteria, so named for the vague collection note that accompanied its original cutting, and prized for musky-sweet, lavender-blue to lilac-violet racemes up to a foot long that open in a strong spring flush with light repeat bloom later in the season. Like other Kentucky wisteria selections it is markedly more restrained than the invasive Chinese and Japanese species, flowering reliably on new wood without the aggressive root suckering that makes those vines a landscape liability. Grow it on a genuinely sturdy, permanent arbor or pergola in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, and prune right after the main spring bloom to control size without sacrificing next year's flowers. It is deer-resistant, heat-tolerant, and easy-care once established.
